keyVerseText: And the sons of Uzzi; Izrahiah: and the sons of Izrahiah; Michael, and Obadiah, and Joel, Ishiah, five: all of them chief men.
rootMeaning: The name יִשִּׁיָּה (Yishshîyâh) derives from the Hebrew root נָשָׁה (nâshâh), meaning to lend or be a creditor, combined with the divine element יָהּ (Yah), a shortened form of Jehovah. Thus, the literal meaning is "Jehovah will lend" or "Yahweh will provide as a lender." This root sense conveys not only the act of lending but also God's gracious provision and sustaining support, emphasizing a relational dynamic of divine generosity rather than mere financial transaction.
usageInScripture: The term יִשִּׁיָּה appears seven times in the Old Testament, primarily as a proper name for five different Israelite men, including warriors, tribal leaders, and Levites. Translations vary slightly—rendered as Ishiah, Isshiah, Ishijah, or Jesiah—reflecting a consistent recognition of the name's identity rather than a conceptual term. The consistent use as a personal name highlights its role in identifying individuals connected to key moments and tribes in Israel’s history rather than as a common noun or verb.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the meaning "Jehovah will lend" affirms God's role as the ultimate provider and sustainer for His people. It reminds believers that all resources, strength, and support are ultimately lent by God, who is faithful to supply their needs. This name, borne by multiple faithful Israelites, symbolizes the trustworthiness of God as a lender who does not withhold but generously equips His servants. In the Christian faith, this underscores the grace and provision of God through Christ, who lends us righteousness and life, enabling us to serve and endure.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 7:3, Ishiah is named among the five sons of Izrahiah, described as "all of them chief men." The presence of the name Ishiah here emphasizes the leadership and prominence of those who carry the meaning "Jehovah will lend." This contributes to the verse by highlighting that God's provision and lending are foundational to the strength and governance of Israel’s tribal leaders, encouraging trust in divine support for communal and spiritual leadership.
